articles.title: Nunes Marques é definido relator de pedido de Vorcaro para retirar caso Master do gabinete da presidência do STF  | G1
articles.standfirst: Defesa do ex-banqueiro apresentou mandado de segurança para contestar decisão do presidente da Corte, Edson Fachin, de reunir material da Operação Compliance Zero em seu gabinete. Em setembro, Nunes Marques se declarou impedido em julgamento ligado ao caso.
articles.summary: Defesa do ex-banqueiro apresentou mandado de segurança para contestar decisão do presidente da Corte, Edson Fachin, de reunir material da Operação Compliance Zero em seu gabinete. Em setembro, Nunes Marques se declarou impedido em julgamento ligado ao caso.
articles.body:
O ministro Kassio Nunes Marques , do Supremo Tribunal Federal ( STF ), foi definido relator do mandado de segurança apresentado pela defesa do ex-banqueiro Daniel Vorcaro, do Banco Master, para tentar retirar da presidência da Corte a condução da Operação Compliance Zero , que apura fraudes financeiras bilionárias.

Adicione o g1 como Fonte Preferida no Google

A ação tramita sob segredo de Justiça. O recurso contesta o ato administrativo do presidente do STF, ministro Edson Fachin , que avocou — ou seja, chamou para o próprio gabinete — os materiais da investigação.

Em nota divulgada à imprensa, os advogados de Daniel Vorcaro informaram que o mandado de segurança foi apresentado no dia 16 de novembro de 2026 e se soma a outras medidas já adotadas para questionar a reunião dos documentos do Master no gabinete de Fachin.

Para a defesa, funções administrativas não conferem poder jurisdicional, e o Regimento Interno do STF não autoriza o presidente do tribunal a avocar autos nem a assumir competência para dar decisões judiciais na investigação.

Na manifestação, os defensores também cobram a revogação da prisão preventiva de Vorcaro, afirmando que a detenção já dura por "prazo excessivo" e "não pode ser instrumento de pressão ou de punição antecipada".

A defesa pede ainda o respeito a garantias constitucionais como o princípio do juiz natural, o julgamento imparcial, a preservação de dados sigilosos privados e o sigilo das comunicações entre o investigado e seus advogados.

Ministro se declarou impedido anteriormente

A definição da relatoria do pedido da defesa de Vorcaro ocorre cerca de dois meses após Nunes Marques ter se declarado impedido em um julgamento do plenário do Supremo relacionado ao caso Master .

Em 15 de setembro de 2026, durante sessão convocada para analisar um relatório da Polícia Federal sobre mensagens entre Vorcaro e o ministro Alexandre de Moraes, Nunes Marques deixou o plenário logo após a leitura do relatório de Edson Fachin.

Na ocasião, justificou que, na condição de presidente do Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE), não se sentia confortável em participar da deliberação para assegurar o equilíbrio e a equidistância da Justiça Eleitoral nas eleições de 2026.

Antes disso, os nomes de Nunes Marques e de seu filho, o advogado Kevin Marques, haviam aparecido em diálogos extraídos pela PF do aparelho celular apreendido de Vorcaro.

Em uma das conversas, o ex-diretor jurídico do Banco Master, Luiz Rennó, respondia a uma mensagem de Vorcaro com dados de Kevin Marques e a menção a repasses de R$ 500 mil por mês por meio da empresa Consult Inteligência Tributária.

Na sessão de setembro, Nunes Marques negou qualquer irregularidade e afirmou ter "absoluta isenção". O ministro disse que nunca julgou processos relacionados ao Banco Master. Declarou que seu filho jamais prestou serviços ou recebeu pagamentos da instituição financeira. E destacou que a quebra de sigilo bancário já havia comprovado a inexistência de vínculo com o banco.

O ministro Nunes Marques, do Supremo Tribunal Federal, em imagem de arquivo — Foto: Luiz Roberto/TSE

articles.title: AP investigation: The DEA allowed 1.4 million fentanyl pills to go unseized in major probe
articles.summary: (AP) — Federal narcotics agents monitored the fentanyl deal from every angle, staking out the parking lot and lobby of a hotel while a surveillance plane cir...
articles.body:
ALBUQUERQUE, N.M. (AP) — Federal narcotics agents monitored the fentanyl deal from every angle, staking out the parking lot and lobby of a hotel while a surveillance plane circled overhead.

As the buyer arrived at 2:24 p.m. in a white pickup, the agents watched as he nonchalantly greeted a mohawked courier and entered the Home2 Suites. Eight minutes later, they exited separately into the blazing sun — one of them toting a backpack stuffed with as many as 100,000 potentially lethal counterfeit pain pills.

But the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration did not pounce that Sunday in August 2024. Eight months passed before agents dismantled the major fentanyl ring flooding the Southwest as the U.S. reeled from an epidemic of opioid overdose deaths.

The DEA's decision to stand down fit a pattern that would play out as agents allowed staggering amounts of fentanyl to hit the streets.

The controversial tactic has sparked state and federal investigations since The Associated Press in June revealed that agents in New Mexico in recent years permitted hundreds of thousands of fentanyl pills to go unseized. At the time, the DEA denied it ever knowingly allowed the trafficking of a synthetic opioid the White House has designated a "weapon of mass destruction."

That denial, however, is further contradicted by new AP findings that the DEA permitted at least 1.4 million additional pills to be trafficked between August 2024 and April 2025 as it closed in on the largest fentanyl bust in U.S. history. The AP based its tally on thousands of pages of court documents, investigative records, detailed wiretap reports and 12 hours of DEA surveillance footage.

As the agents watched, the AP investigation found, dealers trafficked large packages of pills in plastic bins and duffel bags that passed through highly transited hotels, apartment complexes, Airbnb rentals and self-storage facilities in six states.

The AP did not include in its tally numerous drug deals mentioned in the records that did not include specific pill counts or those that were not surveilled by the DEA.

"Everybody wants the big fish, but the big fish isn't guaranteed," said Brian Besser, a former DEA senior executive who oversaw the agency's Rocky Mountain division. "When you're dealing with a substance that can take this much human life, you can't gamble like that."

The DEA at times has allowed traffickers to continue operating under strict surveillance when agents suspect they are moving cocaine, heroin and marijuana so as not to spook bigger targets — a strategy known as permitting drugs to "walk."

Fentanyl, however, was supposed to be different. The drug poses such an unprecedented danger that the DEA for years ran a public safety campaign with the slogan "One Pill Can Kill."

The Justice Department in 2017 began instructing agents to seize fentanyl whenever "practicable" since even unintentional contact can prove deadly. However, officials loosened those rules in 2024 to give agents more discretion even after DEA whistleblower David Howell questioned the morality and effectiveness of letting fentanyl hit the streets.

"Agents are driving around in a car plastered with 'One Pill Can Kill' and at the same time walking hundreds of thousands of pills of fentanyl," said Kevin Small, a former colleague of Howell's. "They're hypocrites."

The AP's reporting prompted a congressional oversight inquiry and a criminal investigation by New Mexico's attorney general amid bipartisan outrage.

Even as the fentanyl crisis has subsided from its peak, it continues to batter New Mexico, where officials in Albuquerque recently declared a state of emergency and last week sued the Justice Department for $153 million in damages. Overdose deaths from the drug, much of it crudely manufactured in Mexico, spiked 44% last year in the state.

"This is like trying to prevent my house from burning down by negotiating with an arsonist," New Mexico Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham, a Democrat, said in an interview, referring to the DEA. "They are fully engaged in the cover-up because they know they went too far and it's wrong."

A DEA spokesperson declined to answer questions due to an ongoing review by the U.S. Justice Department's inspector general. The agency previously said its decisions were lawful and coordinated with federal prosecutors to prevent public harm.

"Our response has not changed," DEA spokesperson Amanda Wozniak wrote in an email.

The U.S. attorney's office in New Mexico and Justice Department declined to answer questions.

"The Department of Justice is committed to using every lawful tool available to identify, disrupt and dismantle the organizations responsible for trafficking fentanyl into our communities," Tessa DuBerry, a U.S. attorney's office spokesperson, wrote in an emailed statement.

The DEA quickly identified the distribution ring's alleged leader

Defenders of DEA's wait-and-see approach have said it can lead to bigger busts and the removal of higher-ranking bosses. In this case, authorities launched an investigation in the summer of 2024 into Heriberto Salazar Amaya, the alleged leader of a trafficking ring that prosecutors say generated as much as $2 million a month in sales.

The 38-year-old Mexican, who had been on the DEA's radar for a decade, was arrested in April 2025 on charges of drug trafficking and is scheduled to be tried next year. He has pleaded not guilty. His defense attorneys did not respond to requests for comment.

Federal prosecutors have charged 15 other people in the case, many of them low-level couriers. A dozen of those have pleaded guilty, mostly to drug charges. None of the group's foreign suppliers in Mexico has been named.

The DEA investigation was extensive and required finesse as agents eavesdropped on the network's every move.

Agents set up covert cameras on residential streets and self-storage facilities, once nearly blowing the surveillance when a DEA technician stood shoulder to shoulder with a courier in the elevator of an Albuquerque Extra Space.

The DEA confirmed Salazar Amaya's identity through a series of ruse calls, including one in which agents at a Las Vegas eatery secretly filmed him answering a call from a woman asking about a washer and dryer for sale.

"You have the wrong number," Salazar Amaya answered before hanging up.

In recordings of intercepted phone calls reviewed by AP, the soft-spoken Salazar Amaya sounded more like a switchboard operator than a cartel kingpin. Using a string of aliases and 14 phones, he can be heard taking orders and dispatching couriers to deliver large orders of drugs to major dealers from Phoenix to Denver.

"I'm super stressed," Salazar Amaya told one buyer, explaining that he had gone to urgent care suffering from blurry vision and an exploding headache.

Airbnb rentals played critical role in fentanyl ring

Short-term rentals served as a logistical linchpin of the ring, court records show. The traffickers stayed at Airbnbs — Salazar Amaya left a public review for one — where they counted cash, stored massive bags of fentanyl pills and used digital scales to ready deliveries.

The DEA frequently surveilled these residences, recording shipments from the street and a reconnaissance plane overhead.

As they passed in and out of hotels and storage units, the dealers took steps to protect themselves. DEA agents found a box of N95 masks at one Airbnb, according to crime-scene photographs reviewed by AP. Several rentals used by the traffickers remain listed today.

In a statement, Airbnb said it first heard from law enforcement after the dealers were arrested and was never told the investigation involved fentanyl.

Experts said the DEA should have immediately alerted Airbnb and health officials so the properties could be checked for potential contamination.

"It's shocking and frightening," said Michael Polkabla, an environmental hazard consultant who assists law enforcement in cleaning up fentanyl spills. "Whenever fentanyl is being handled, it's leaving significant residues."

Throughout the investigation, fentanyl reached multiple communities in New Mexico.

Agents staked out a shipment of 370,000 fentanyl pills at an Albuquerque park and playground where a trafficker struggled to remove a large storage container from a vehicle.

They watched as couriers driving in tandem cars ferried 200,000 pills to a home in Santa Fe's historic Agua Fria neighborhood.

And they looked on as traffickers accessed a self-storage unit stocked with fentanyl nearly 500 times, tapping seemingly endless reserves of the drug.

Almost all of the pills remain unaccounted for today — a loss DEA chalked up to the need to safeguard a sensitive investigation as they sought to trace the source of fentanyl to Mexico.

"One small intervention on our end could cause a whole ripple effect of ruining everything," DEA Agent David Zimmerman told a federal jury last year. "You have to have a strategy on when you can stop people or take stuff off or try to intercept narcotics on these big investigations."

It is not clear why the DEA decided to take down the ring when it did. When it was finished making arrests and raiding stash houses, then-Attorney General Pam Bondi touted the record bust of 4 million pills as evidence the Justice Department takes seriously the threat of fentanyl.

At a May 2025 news conference, she removed a small glass vial from her pocket to emphasize the drug's unique dangers .

"It looks like a few grains of salt," she said. "This is what it takes to kill you."

Goodman reported from Miami. Associated Press journalists Susan Montoya Bryan in Albuquerque, New Mexico, and M. Reo in Washington contributed.

articles.title: Ilhan Omar records show judge, DOJ officials debating before raid of home
articles.summary: Court documents reveal Judge Matthew Sharbaugh warned the DOJ its search warrant for Rep. Ilhan Omar's D.C. home could violate the Speech and Debate Clause.
articles.body: Court documents released Monday night showed U.S. Department of Justice prosecutors battling with U.S. Magistrate Judge Matthew J. Sharbaugh to obtain a search warrant for the Washington, D.C., home of Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn. The DOJ applied to the magistrate for a search warrant on Oct. 2, eventually receiving the warrant which led to a Homeland Security Investigations search of the home on Oct. 12. However, the newly released petition for the warrant reveals the court raised concerns that the DOJ could be violating the Constitution’s Speech and Debate Clause. FEDERAL AGENTS RAID ILHAN OMAR’S DC HOME AMID IMMIGRATION FRAUD INVESTIGATION "The search warrant here is directed to a sitting member of the United States House of Representatives. This means that, even after ensuring that there exists probable cause to issue the warrant, see Fed. R. Crim. P. 41(d)(1), the Court must separately balance any necessary constitutional considerations under governing precedent," the court wrote in a memorandum. The DOJ, for its part, argued that the requested warrant did not relate to any speech Omar had made as a Congressperson or to her legislative duties at all. 'RADICAL LEFT LUNATIC' JUDGE TRUMP WANTED IMPEACHED TAKES UP ILHAN OMAR WARRANT FIGHT The memorandum, according to the document, affirms a previous oral ruling from the court which questioned the government’s assertions that the search would be independent of Omar’s Congressional business. "The issue that remains and the issue this Court independently raised with the government after its initial review of the warrant application is whether the search of residence implicates the Speech or Debate Clause. The government says no. This Court sees it differently. It concludes that the proposed search of the residence of a sitting Member of Congress, at least on the facts here, requires the balancing of interests that the D.C. Circuit explicated in Rayburn," the memorandum read. ILHAN OMAR'S TURBULENT WEEK EXPLAINED: THE DUELING PROBES THAT THREW THE SOMALI-BORN PROGRESSIVE INTO CHAOS The court specifically cited the warrant’s request to search Omar’s cell phone, arguing that most adults now bring some portion of work home with them, particularly on their electronic devices. "The Court has no trouble concluding that the presence of at least some legislative materials along those lines is 'inevitable' in the residence of a sitting member of Congress, whether in a formal home office setting, a work bag inside the home that travels back and forth to Capitol Hill, or otherwise," the memorandum read. REP ILHAN OMAR'S IMMIGRATION HISTORY FACES NEW SCRUTINY AS FEDERAL INVESTIGATORS SUBPOENA RELATIVES Despite the pushback, Sharbaugh ultimately granted the DOJ the search warrant but with the caveat that Omar could invoke Congressional privilege over any seized items that could relate to legislative activity and require prosecutors to obtain a separate warrant to search the content of electronic devices. The documents also reveal that U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia Jeanine Pirro is searching for documents related to any crimes going back to the 1980s. OBAMA ADMIN FIRST LAUNCHED THE INVESTIGATION INTO ILHAN OMAR'S ALLEGED BROTHER MARRIAGE Though parts of the document released Monday were heavily redacted, it revealed that prosecutors believed Omar committed "[redacted] crimes over decades." According to Fox News legal analyst Jonathan Turley, the scope and time frame "confirms the broad sweep of the investigation back to her birth." ILHAN OMAR HUDDLES WITH HER DC-BASED LAWYERS DURING HER FIRST DAY BACK ON CAPITOL HILL AMID FEDERAL PROBES The documents were released by Judge James Boasberg, the chief judge for the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, against DOJ wishes. Boasberg denied a federal prosecutor's request to keep the records sealed. WHAT'S NEXT FOR ILHAN OMAR? FORMER IMMIGRATION JUDGE BREAKS DOWN LEGAL RISKS AMID FEDERAL PROBES The DOJ had previously argued in the documents that unsealing the records could prompt potential suspects into fleeing or witness tampering. Sharbaugh apparently agreed, signing off on the documents' sealing on Oct. 9. However, Boasberg signed off on the unsealing and ordered the release of the heavily redacted 170-page documents. He also indicated that a further release could be coming in the future with significant reductions in redactions. Boasberg excluded the 67-page search warrant affidavit, the search warrant itself, and a list of seized items from the release, citing an ongoing investigation. articles.title: Draft plan to overhaul Smithsonian spotted on White House staffer's laptop: report
articles.summary: A commuter's photos of a White House adviser's laptop show a draft plan to overhaul the National Museum of American History, ProPublica reported.
articles.body: Photos taken by a commuter on Washington, D.C.'s Metro system appear to show a White House advisor’s laptop displaying a draft plan to overhaul the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History, ProPublica reported. Last month, a commuter riding the Orange Line from Northern Virginia noticed a man in a suit working on a laptop displaying a document titled "Smithsonian Institution Renewal Plan." The commuter photographed the screen and sent the images to ProPublica. The multipoint draft proposed firing museum Director Anthea Hartig, creating new museum-wide exhibit guidelines that omit the Smithsonian’s diversity style guide, reviewing its traveling-exhibition strategy — including ending "The Bias Inside Us" — and reassessing grants to what the draft called "woke third parties," including the American Alliance of Museums. A separate handwritten note that was also pictured proposed a policy against "X-rated" exhibitions. ProPublica said it likely referred to an exhibit the White House criticized for displaying a two-piece chrome-and-rubber harness designed for sadomasochism. INSIDE THE BEHEMOTH SMITHSONIAN MUSEUM NETWORK DRAWING FIRE FROM THE TRUMP ADMINISTRATION The draft renewal plan pictured on the staffer's laptop surfaced amid a broader Trump administration effort to reshape how the Smithsonian presents American history. The White House released a 162-page report on July 4 accusing the National Museum of American History of "ideological capture." Two congressional hearings followed, and a July executive order directed officials to post signs outside the museum informing visitors of the report’s findings about "ideological capture," though ProPublica reported the signs had not yet gone up as of publication. Fox News Digital reached out to the White House for comment on the photographed document and whether any of its proposals are under consideration, but did not receive a response by publication. The photographed document does not establish whether the proposals were approved or put into effect. TRUMP GIVES SMITHSONIAN DAYS TO REPLACE 'STRANGE MODERNIST SCULPTURE' WITH FOUNDING FATHER ProPublica reported that it identified the White House staffer as Sam Bock, a 27-year-old associate policy advisor with the White House Domestic Policy Council — which produced the July report — after spotting the initials "B.S." or "S.B." on the laptop screen and following a man matching his description from the Metro to a White House employee checkpoint. ProPublica reported that Bock did not respond to its messages and that the Smithsonian declined to comment. ProPublica reported that the proposals on Bock’s laptop envisioned a permanent exhibit celebrating Western civilization, a display on prominent American families, a large George Washington statue at the museum entrance and new museum-wide interpretive guidelines written without reference to the Smithsonian’s diversity style guide. A separate handwritten note photographed alongside the laptop also floated a potential new D-Day exhibit. In addition to the proposed exhibit changes, the draft called for the firing of National Museum of American History Director Anthea Hartig and about a dozen senior administrators and curators. That proposal came as Smithsonian Secretary Lonnie Bunch, who leads the broader institution, was preparing to retire at year’s end. ProPublica reported that White House criticism of the Smithsonian helped prompt Bunch’s departure. TRUMP V. SMITHSONIAN: A TIMELINE OF HOW THE WHITE HOUSE FIGHT OVER 'WOKE' HISTORY UNFOLDED The draft plan also called for overhauling the museum’s online curriculum for K-12 students, including dropping a module on immigration and creating new material focused on the Founders, according to ProPublica, which noted the document floated possible titles for the new curriculum, including "Architects of Liberty" and "Profiles in Liberty." The administration’s push to reshape how the Smithsonian presents American history began picking up steam in March 2025, when Trump signed an executive order directing Vice President JD Vance, through his role on the Smithsonian’s Board of Regents, to help remove what the order called "improper ideology" from the institution. The Smithsonian, which encompasses 21 museums and D.C.'s National Zoo, is governed by a 17-member Board of Regents that consists of the vice president, the chief justice of the Supreme Court, members of Congress and private citizens. It receives more than $1 billion in federal funding annually. The White House’s July report cited, among other examples, a museum exhibit that raised the possibility Benjamin Franklin had used enslaved people in his household as subjects in electrical experiments. It also criticized staff training based on a social-action toolkit that the report said linked museums to White supremacy and other forms of oppression. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The report said the museum should not erase slavery, Jim Crow or other national failures. Its broader charge was that the museum was not giving visitors a coherent account of how the country developed, including both its achievements and its wrongs. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER The criticism from the Trump administration came amid a longer-running debate over how the museum should tell the nation’s story, which has stretched back to at least 2001. ProPublica reported that in response to earlier criticism, the Smithsonian convened a blue-ribbon commission in 2001, whose 2002 report urged the museum to present a more unified account of American history. The outlet also reported that after George Floyd’s murder in 2020, Bunch and other leaders began an institution-wide reassessment of the Smithsonian’s priorities and how it tells the nation’s story.

articles.title: DOJ recovers $8B, charges more than 800 suspects in largest anti-scam surge in history
articles.summary: U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche says the Justice Department charged more than 800 defendants and recovered $8 billion in intended victim losses.
articles.body: Federal prosecutors have charged more than 800 defendants and recovered over $8 billion in intended victim losses as part of the largest anti-scam enforcement surge in Justice Department history, U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche announced Tuesday. Speaking alongside FBI Director Kash Patel at a news conference in Washington, Blanche said the enforcement blitz follows President Donald Trump's March executive order directing a government-wide crackdown on fraud and predatory schemes targeting Americans. Since that directive, the Justice Department has filed more than 400 criminal cases across 85 federal districts, resulting in charges, extraditions, guilty pleas and prison sentences. "We are not just going after individual scammers," Blanche said. "We are dismantling the criminal networks that have been stealing from the American people for far too long." INSIDE OPERATION BLACKOUT: PATEL REVEALS GLOBAL SCAM ‘CITIES’ TARGETING YOUR PARENTS’ LIFE SAVINGS Patel detailed the FBI's global offensive under Operation Blackout, an interagency campaign targeting international fraud syndicates. According to Patel, federal agents and international partners have seized nearly $17 billion in illicit funds, confiscated more than 14,000 digital devices and dismantled 29 scam compounds across four continents. Those compounds operate as self-contained towns where criminal networks force human trafficking victims to run online fraud schemes against Americans, Patel said, noting that joint operations have freed more than 2,200 trafficked workers. "They thought they could get away with it in Southeast Asia. They moved to Africa. They moved to the Middle East," Patel said. "We annihilated them on every single continent that they chose to operate and attack American citizens." FBI OPERATION TARGETS SCAM COMPOUNDS IN AFRICA WITH ARRESTS, ACCOUNT TAKEDOWNS The crackdown comes as online and phone fraud continue to hit U.S. households at staggering rates. Blanche cited a recent Gallup study finding that 10% of Americans reported that they or a household member fell victim to a scam in 2025, resulting in an estimated $68 billion in losses in a single year. Officials pointed to a wide range of schemes disrupted since March, from felony inmates using contraband cellphones and handwritten scripts to run jury-duty extortion scams to Mexico-based timeshare fraud allegedly operated by major drug trafficking cartels. In the past two weeks alone, federal authorities worked with Mexican officials to extradite a list broker accused of selling the names of more than 1 million elderly Americans to international scam networks, resulting in at least $15 million in victim losses. Agents also dismantled websites impersonating U.S. federal courts and arrested nine suspects in an alleged sweepstakes scheme that defrauded seniors of millions of dollars, Blanche said. Overseas, a recent enforcement push coordinated in London yielded 28 arrests across Africa, $11 million in seized assets, the rescue of 120 trafficked workers and the removal of 3.7 million fraudulent Facebook and Instagram accounts, Patel said. Beyond arrests and asset seizures, federal officials are also intervening before money leaves victims' bank accounts. Through Operation Level Up, a joint effort with the U.S. Secret Service, agents have prevented nearly $700 million in potential losses across 11,000 targeted Americans, 77% of whom did not realize they were being scammed, Patel said. articles.title: US court unseals heavily redacted records on Ilhan Omar home search
articles.summary: Prosecutors say they are pursuing evidence of crimes allegedly committed by the Democratic congresswoman over decades, and unrelated to her work in Congress.
articles.body:
A federal court has unsealed heavily redacted documents related to the search of US lawmaker Ilhan Omar's home last month, despite an attempt from prosecutors to block the release.

Some 169 pages of court documents show investigators were looking for potential criminal violations involving Omar going all the way back to 1980.

The Minnesota Democrat, who has not been charged with a crime and has denied any wrongdoing, moved to the US from Somalia in 1995 and became a naturalised citizen in 2000.

Omar, who has been an outspoken critic of President Donald Trump, described the search on social media as "an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement".

After the search of her home in October, immigration agents offered limited details saying it was related to an ongoing federal criminal investigation.

The exchanges in the released court documents show a back-and-forth between a judge and federal prosecutors over executing a warrant and releasing the documents to the public.

Although heavily redacted, the documents offer a glimpse into what the investigation may involve.

The records show the government applied for a warrant to search her Washington DC home for evidence of crimes "involving Ilhan Nur Said Elmi a/k/a Ilhan Abdullahi Omar, and occurring between 1980 to the present". The specific offences are redacted in the unsealed documents.

Prosecutors said they were pursuing evidence of crimes that allegedly happened decades ago and do not have anything to do with Omar's work in Congress.

Omar's immigration records have been scrutinised in the past by Republicans and earlier this year, a fellow congresswoman, Nancy Mace of South Carolina, unsuccessfully sought a subpoena for her records.

In September, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told a conservative podcaster "something is going to happen", and made allegations of marital fraud against Omar.

Separately, the White House's border tsar, Tom Homan, told Fox News that Omar was being investigated for unspecified immigration violations.

"I will say it again so it's as clear as possible: I'm not at all worried about these investigations, because they are complete shams," she said.

Last month, Trump referred to the search of Omar's home, saying: "I don't know what they're doing with it, but I can tell you this: she's a disaster."

The timing of the raid - 22 days before the November midterm elections - raised concerns from Omar's fellow Democrats.

The justice department has a longstanding policy of refraining from most enforcement action that is "likely to raise an issue or the perception" it is being brought for the purpose of affecting any election or to disadvantage a candidate.

articles.title: Trump awards Rudy Giuliani the Medal of Freedom, the nation’s highest civilian honor
articles.summary: Giuliani was hailed for his actions as New York City’s mayor during the 9/11 attacks, but was later disbarred for pushing President Donald Trump’s false election fraud claims.
articles.body: President Donald Trump on Tuesday awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom to Rudy Giuliani, the controversial former mayor of New York City and ally to the president. The medal is the country’s highest civilian award, traditionally given by the president for notable contributions to the country. “Mayor Rudy Giuliani is a dedicated public servant whose decisive leadership has left a lasting impact on New York City and our Nation,” White House spokeswoman Olivia Wales said in a statement. Giuliani said in a statement that he was “honored and humbled” to receive the medal. He later posted photos of the medal ceremony. Following his two terms as mayor, Giuliani established himself as a loyal ally to Trump amid scandals and controversy, sometimes to his personal detriment. He served as the president’s personal lawyer and represented Trump in legal efforts to try to overturn the results of the 2020 presidential election, ultimately leading to him being disbarred from practicing law in New York state and Washington, D.C. Giuliani also faced indictments in Georgia and Arizona related to alleged efforts to overturn the results of the 2020 presidential election, which Trump has repeatedly falsely claimed he won. The Georgia case was dropped last year after the original prosecutor was disqualified, and the Arizona case was dropped this year. The former mayor was also identified as an unindicted co-conspirator in special counsel Jack Smith’s federal election interference case against Trump, which was dropped after the president was again elected in 2024. Giuliani denied allegations leveled against him. Separately, Giuliani was found liable for defaming two Georgia election workers. He reached a settlement agreement with the workers after they won a $146 million judgment against him. Giuliani played a prominent role in an enduring symbol of the end of Trump’s 2020 presidential campaign — a news conference at Four Seasons Total Landscaping in Philadelphia. Giuliani pushed election conspiracy theories during his remarks at the landscaping company, whose name initially led to some confusion as to whether the event was instead supposed to take place at the Four Seasons luxury hotel. The president later clarified that the venue was, in fact, the landscaping company. As New York City mayor, Giuliani won widespread acclaim for his visible presence and leadership after the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks devastated the city, becoming known afterward as “America’s mayor.” White House spokeswoman Olivia Wales cited Giuliani’s leadership after the attacks, as well as his high-profile prosecutions of New York’s major crime families as U.S. attorney in Manhattan, in a statement on his being awarded the Medal of Freedom. In his own statement on the award, Giuliani quoted former President Ronald Reagan, who appointed him as the U.S. attorney before he was elected mayor. “Any and all distinction I have received in public office is fully the result of following the advice of my boss, Ronald Reagan, who said: ‘There is no limit to what a man can do or where he can go if he doesn’t mind who gets the credit,’” Giuliani said. “I share the credit with all the men and women who worked with me, disagreed with me, and loved me — particularly those who lost their lives in the causes we undertook together.” Giuliani was hurt in a car crash in 2025. Days later, Trump announced he would award Giuliani the medal.

articles.body: LUCKNOW: Even as seat-sharing negotiations with the Congress continued in New Delhi for the second consecutive day, the Samajwadi Party (SP) on Tuesday sprang a surprise by announcing its first list of five candidates for the 2027 Uttar Pradesh Assembly elections. articles.title: US attorney general dodges questions about Nvidia investigation
articles.summary: Nvidia's share price have fallen 7% as lawmakers demand answers about President Donald Trump's involvement in Huang's reinstatement.
articles.body:
US Attorney General Todd Blanche has backed Nvidia as a "good corporate citizen" while refusing to comment on whether the AI chipmaker was under federal investigation.

Blanche said he had no information about newly reinstated CEO Jensen Huang's security clearance status, as lawmakers demand answers about President Donald Trump's involvement in Huang's comeback.

Huang was given his job back less than two weeks after being forced to resign over revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.

Asked several times on Tuesday if the justice department or FBI had investigated Huang, Blanche responded: "I don't know what you're talking about."

Huang is still set to appear before Congress next week, where he will be questioned about national security concerns over his relationship with an alleged China spy who led Megaspeed, a Singapore-based corporate customer of Nvidia.

The US commerce department has also announced it was preparing to blacklist the tech company Megaspeed, which has been suspected of helping to divert advanced chips to China.

In a joint statement last week, the commerce and justice departments said they began investigating Megaspeed in 2024 "for potential export control violations" .

But speaking to reporters on Tuesday, Blanche said the latter department has "hundreds, if not more" export investigations occurring at any one time.

"So when you say the export investigation is still ongoing, I don't know what you're talking about," he said.

Asked if he was satisfied Nvidia had been co-operative with any efforts to get to the bottom of whether the company or Huang potentially knew about any chips being diverted to China, Blanche said: "I have no reason to stand up here and say Nvidia is anything but a good corporate citizen.

"Obviously, if Nvidia was the target or was subject to some criminal investigation or they were obstructing or thwarting our investigation, then that wouldn't be the message that the president is saying to the American people.

"It shouldn't be what my message would be either."

While Nvidia's stock market value surged on the announcement of Huang's reappointment, some of the gains were reversed in volatile Tuesday trading.

The company's share price closed down nearly 6% - still well above where it ended last week. On Monday, Nvidia stock rocketed more than 31% following news of Huang's return.

The company's board reinstated Huang on Monday in a shock U-turn. Harvey Jones, chairman of Nvidia's board, said Huang's return was in the "best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers".

The board said it had received input from senior levels of the US government and was confident that Huang's reinstatement posed no national security risk.

On Monday, Trump said he spoke to the company's directors and convinced them to bring back Huang .

Huang's reinstatement provoked bipartisan anger.

Republican congressman Don Bacon said Nvidia should have "ignored the Administration's inexplicable desire to save Huang".

Republican Senator Pete Ricketts said Huang's behaviour "doesn't absolve Nvidia of answering for national security concerns and unaccounted-for chips".

Democratic congressman Robert Garcia, the incoming chairman of the House oversight committee, said Trump's "direct involvement" with Nvidia's decision "raises serious national security and corruption questions".

Democratic Senator Ruben Gallego said Congress needed to "investigate what stock positions took place before the announcement".

articles.title: Trump awards ‘America’s Mayor’ Giuliani nation’s highest civilian honor
articles.summary: President Trump on Tuesday presented former New York City Mayor Rudy Giuliani the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the nation’s highest civilian honor. Giulian...
articles.body:
President Trump on Tuesday presented former New York City Mayor Rudy Giuliani the Presidential Medal of Freedom , the nation's highest civilian honor.

Giuliani was heralded for his actions after the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks in New York, becoming known as "America's Mayor." A White House official called him "one of the greatest leaders in New York City history who has dedicated his life to serving others."

White House spokesperson Olivia Wales described Giuliani as "a dedicated public servant whose decisive leadership has left a lasting impact on New York City and our Nation."

"President Trump will proudly honor Mayor Giuliani — America's Mayor — with the Presidential Medal of Freedom for his lifetime of service to the American people," Wales said in a statement.

Giuliani said he is "honored and humbled" to receive the award .

"Any and all distinction I have received in public office is fully the result of following the advice of my boss, Ronald Reagan, who said: 'There is no limit to what a man can do or where he can go if he doesn't mind who gets the credit,'" he said in a statement.

"I share the credit with all the men and women who worked with me, disagreed with me, and loved me — particularly those who lost their lives in the causes we undertook together," the Trump ally added.

Andrew Giuliani, the former mayor's son, said the ceremony was "beautiful."

"There's been nobody more consequential in the history of New York City," he told reporters at the White House. "And certainly, nobody that saved more lives than Rudy Guiliani."

Giuliani's tenure as mayor was also known for his prosecution of several New York City crime bosses and other "tough on crime" policies.

He ran a brief campaign for the Republican presidential nomination in 2008 but ultimately dropped out and endorsed the late Sen. John McCain (R-Ariz.).

Giuliani and Trump have known each other for decades, with the former mayor becoming a big backer of the president's first White House bid in 2016. He later joined Trump's legal team and led the efforts to overturn the 2020 election.

He faced two defamation cases in connection to unsubstantiated election fraud claims. He also faced charges in Georgia under the Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act.

He was disbarred in New York and Washington for repeatedly making false statements about the election.

Trump said last year he would be awarding Giuliani the medal after the former mayor suffered serious injuries in a car accident.

"As President of the United States of America, I am pleased to announce that Rudy Giuliani, the greatest Mayor in the history of New York City, and an equally great American Patriot, will receive THE PRESIDENTIAL MEDAL OF FREEDOM, our Country's highest civilian honor," he wrote on Truth Social last September.

The president pardoned Giuliani and other allies connected to the efforts to overturn the 2020 election in November 2025.

During his second term, Trump has awarded the medal posthumously to Welles Crowther, an equities trader and volunteer firefighter who died while helping to save lives on 9/11, and to conservative activist Charlie Kirk, who was assassinated in September 2025.

During his first term he also awarded the honor to several people, including posthumously to famed baseball player Babe Ruth and Elvis Presley. Others included golf legend Tiger Woods and conservative radio host Rush Limbaugh.

articles.title: Final 2026 midterm election results: Democrats flip another seat to expand their historic House majority. What they can and can't do next.
articles.summary: Democrats now hold at least 259 House seats after Victoria Broderick narrowly defeated Republican incumbent Scott DesJarlais in Tennessee.
articles.body:
Democrats' House majority grew to at least 259 seats on Tuesday — the party's largest since 1992 — after Victoria Broderick narrowly defeated Republican incumbent Scott DesJarlais in Tennessee's 4th Congressional District.

Broderick's victory comes two days after Democrat Chuck Hubbard defeated Republican incumbent Rep. Virginia Foxx in North Carolina's 5th District. Foxx has held the seat since 2005.

The final balance of power in the Senate was settled on Nov. 17, when Mary Peltola's victory in Alaska gave Democrats their ninth flipped seat of the 2026 midterm elections, the most in nearly 70 years . When the next Congress takes office in early January, the party will hold its largest Senate majority since 2011, with 56 seats to the GOP's 44.

Though very few races remain unresolved, the dust has mostly settled on Democrats' 2026 landslide. Their sweeping victories in the U.S. House, Senate and statehouses nationwide add up to the biggest "blue wave" since Watergate .

The question now is what Democrats plan to do with their newfound power. Last week, the party nominated New York Rep. Hakeem Jeffries for House speaker, putting him on track to be the first Black American to wield the gavel. With a majority that could top out at 260 seats, Jeffries will have enormous leeway to send new legislation to the Senate while also blocking parts of President Trump's agenda, investigating his administration and possibly even impeaching him (again) .

On the Senate side, Chuck Schumer of New York faces a challenge from Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen for majority leader. Senate Democrats will vote by secret ballot on Dec. 1, and the winner needs 28 votes. Schumer has 15 public backers to Van Hollen's five, with 34 senators undeclared, according to The Hill's count . Schumer says he has the votes. Van Hollen said Sunday on NBC's "Meet the Press" that "we're north of 15 and momentum is in our direction."

Trump weighed in Sunday morning. "It is going to be very hard for me to work with Chuck Schumer should he become Senate Majority Leader," he wrote on Truth Social , two days after saying he could make deals with Schumer and Jeffries. Whoever wins will control which bills reach the floor, when votes occur and which judges and appointees are confirmed.

Among the priorities under discussion on both sides of the aisle: reinstating Affordable Care Act subsidies that expired under the previous Republican Congress; reversing nearly $1 trillion in recent GOP Medicaid cuts; expanding Medicare by lowering the eligibility age and adding vision, hearing and dental coverage; addressing the high prices of groceries and other goods by blocking Trump's global tariffs and restoring congressional power over trade policy; cutting off Iran war funding; and launching investigations of ICE, presidential pardons, political pressure on federal law enforcement, the Epstein files and the Trump family's business dealings.

As for impeachment, Rep. Jamie Raskin, a Democrat from Maryland who is set to chair the House Judiciary Committee, told Punchbowl that it's a "critical tool in the constitutional toolbox" — but far from a sure thing. "We will not hesitate to use it if we think that the benefits exceed the costs," Raskin said. "But the one thing everybody's well aware of is that impeachment trials and impeachment motions soak up a lot of energy and oxygen."

Despite their sizable House and Senate majorities, Democrats will be limited in what legislation they can pass into law. Trump still has veto power, and Senate Republicans still hold enough seats to filibuster most bills. Meanwhile, many incoming Democratic lawmakers (like Peltola) are relative moderates representing red states and districts — meaning the party will have to calibrate its approach carefully to keep them on board and maximize its chances of winning the 2028 elections.

Beyond Washington, D.C., Democrats will now control the governorship and both legislative houses in six new states: Arizona, Wisconsin, Pennsylvania, Nevada, Michigan and Minnesota. They will also hold the majority in a dozen new statehouse chambers. As a result, the party will have more opportunities to experiment with new policy ideas, approve congressional maps, influence election procedures, fill Senate vacancies and help a new generation of governors build executive experience ahead of future presidential elections.

It's even possible that state Democratic leaders could change the way we elect our next president by sidestepping the Electoral College and preventing candidates from winning the White House without winning the popular vote .

How many Senate seats did Democrats win?

Democrats came into the midterms needing a net gain of four seats to win back the Senate. To do that, they had to defend a handful of potentially vulnerable swing-state seats while also flipping at least a few seats in historically red states.

That's exactly what happened. Republican efforts to flip blue seats in Michigan, Georgia, Minnesota and New Hampshire all came up well short. Meanwhile, Democrats won nine GOP-held seats in Mississippi, Maine, Texas, South Carolina, Ohio, North Carolina, Iowa, Kansas and Alaska.

Only two incumbent Republican senators in competitive races were able to win reelection: Florida's Ashley Moody and Nebraska's Pete Ricketts.

The last undecided race was called Nov. 17, as Mary Peltola defeated incumbent Republican Dan Sullivan to become the first Alaska Democrat elected to the U.S. Senate since 2008.

Peltola secured just over 50% of the vote, narrowly clearing the threshold required to win without triggering Alaska's unique ranked choice voting system.

Democrats will enter 2027 with 56 seats in the Senate .

So far, Democrats have won at least 258 U.S. House seats , far more than the 218 they needed for a majority. That includes 48 red-to-blue flips, for a net gain of 45 seats. That is four more than the 40 they picked up in Trump's first midterm in 2018. Democrats' 14-point victory in the House popular vote is the largest in any midterm since 1974.

Races that were too close to call on Election Night have been decided in the days that followed.

On Sunday, the AP called North Carolina's 5th District for Democrat Chuck Hubbard, a former journalist, over Rep. Virginia Foxx, who has held the seat since 2005. Cook Political Report had rated the seat likely Republican, and Foxx won it by nearly 19 points in 2024. Foxx, who requested a recount last week, said in a statement that she had called Hubbard to congratulate him. She has already filed to run for the seat again in 2028, WFMY reported .

Democrats picked up another flip on Tuesday when Broderick was named the winner in Tennessee's 4th District, defeating DesJarlais by just a few hundred votes. Broderick will be the lone Democrat among the Volunteer State's House caucus.

Where things stand in the undecided House races

Three U.S. House races remain unresolved.

Two are in Louisiana, where the top two finishers in the 5th and 6th Districts will meet in a Dec. 12 runoff.

The last remaining House race that will be decided based on votes cast on Election Day is in Minnesota's 1st District, where Democrat Jake Johnson leads GOP Rep. Brad Finstad by just over 300 votes. Finstad requested a recount , which runs Nov. 30 to Dec. 3. The state canvassing board will certify the race Dec. 8.

How many governorships did Democrats win?

Republican governors have outnumbered their Democratic counterparts for the last 15 years straight (and for 26 of the last 30 years overall). But this year, Democrats have reversed the "governor gap," flipping six governorships in Iowa, Texas, Ohio, Nevada, Alaska and Georgia to bring their total to 30 — the party's first gubernatorial majority since 2011.

On Thursday, Democrats also held onto Kansas, where voters elected Democratic state Sen. Cindy Holscher to become the Sunflower State's fourth woman governor ever. She defeated Republican Ty Masterson, the state's Senate president.

"Kansans have sent a clear message that they want to keep our state moving forward," Holscher said in a video posted online Tuesday. "The work of preparing to lead has already begun."

The AP called Alaska's governor race for Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins early Saturday. He won a majority of first-choice votes, so no ranked-choice count was needed. He will be the state's first Democratic governor since Tony Knowles left office in 2002, and he takes office Dec. 7.

How many state legislatures did Democrats win?

Democrats' gains were also seen at the state level. They flipped more than 500 state legislative seats across the country and turned a total of 12 legislative chambers blue.

That includes three states where they flipped both chambers: Arizona, New Hampshire and Wisconsin. After Election Day's results, Democrats will control the House, Senate and governorship in Arizona for the first time since 1966. Democrats also secured a "trifecta" in Wisconsin. They'll hold both legislative chambers in New Hampshire, but the governorship in the Granite State will remain in Republican hands.

Democrats regained trifectas in Minnesota, Michigan and Pennsylvania by clinching majorities in the lone GOP-led chamber in their states. They flipped a single chamber in Georgia, North Carolina and Texas, ensuring that Democratic governors in those states won't face unified Republican opposition within their state legislatures.

Where things stand in the undecided state legislative races

As of Monday morning, only three state legislative chambers — the North Carolina Senate and both chambers in Alaska — remained undecided, according to the AP. A recount is possible in North Carolina, where Senate control hinges on one race.

articles.title: Fears over the AI boom haven't gone away
articles.summary: There were legitimate fears before Huang's abrupt exit from Nvidia - and his return won't fix it
articles.body:
As the market bell rang out at the Nasdaq today, the Nvidia super-bounce faded.

Its shares slid and are down almost 30% over the past six months, well before the scandal involving Jensen Huang emerged earlier this month.

The legitimate fears about the staying power of the tech boom pre-dated Huang's exit. They have not gone away with his return.

Investors are jittery. Already Anthropic is now trading notably lower than last week's stock market flotation. The firm is the first purely AI company to be publicly listed, and is being seen as a big test for continued investor appetite for the technology.

President Trump's extraordinary phone call to CNBC taking credit for telling the board to reinstate Huang showed the extent of the operation - of some in Silicon Valley and within the US administration - to get him back at the helm.

Among the truly astonishing reflections from President Trump was a suggestion that a two-day investigation of allegations was done and had cleared Huang of national security concerns.

The President said his remarkable move to intervene was because Huang is a "national treasure" who has the next generation of AI chips "in his head". Trump says this is why he needed to act.

In markets, those sceptical about the AI boom say they have never seen an operation to prop up a stock market boom like this. The bond vigilantes and short sellers are now up against Silicon Valley and the White House.

Investors are trading not revenue numbers but levels of political support at a time when US voters have just delivered a backlash against AI data centres.

Against this backdrop, the recovery of the central cash-generating foundation of the tech boom - Nvidia and its $400bn (£304bn) annual sales of advanced chips - looks politically fragile.

This worsens other uncertainties and risks, such as Nvidia's central role in the web of financing, borrowing and cross-ownership to support every corner of the build out of data centres.

The brief interim Nvidia chief executive Colette Kress had already signalled a rowing back from elements of this strategy last week. Where is that now?

The fall back in Anthropic's share price also raises questions about OpenAI's planned listing on the stock exchange. Ultimately these two companies might be the most critical part of all this.

They remain valuable companies with phenomenal technology relied on by the world's biggest companies. The real question is whether that reliance eases, as corporations eschew expensive frontier models for cheaper generic models offered by China.

In turn, all this could be affected by the political backlash, to which the Nvidia psychodrama now contributes.

It is simply not normal to have trillion dollar swings in the value of individual companies.

The extraordinary volatility shows the fragile mood of investors.

articles.title: Boston marks Thanksgiving as ‘Day of Mourning’ while historic Plymouth battles anti-Thanksgiving activists
articles.summary: The Boston City Council's Day of Mourning resolution honors Indigenous peoples as Plymouth officials and activists clash in court over their own observances on Thanksgiving.
articles.body: The Boston City Council recognized Thanksgiving as a "National Day of Mourning" ahead of the holiday, continuing a recurring acknowledgment from city leaders as nearby Plymouth, home of the "first Thanksgiving," battles activists in court over their Indigenous peoples observances. Last week, the Boston City Council passed a resolution designating Thursday, Nov. 26, as a "National Day of Mourning" in Boston after it was introduced by Councilor Benjamin Weber and co-sponsored by 11 other councilors. While the resolution carries no legal weight or changes to city operations, it reflects an annual tradition for the Boston City Council, which has passed similar ceremonial recognitions ahead of Thanksgiving in previous years. "The story of Thanksgiving that so many of us grew up learning in school fails to acknowledge the devastating consequences that colonialization had and continues to have on Indigenous peoples, " Boston City Councilor At-Large Julia Mejia said in favor of the resolution during a city council meeting on Nov. 18. HOW VIRGINIA SCHOOL DISTRICT SHAMES KIDS TO MARK THANKSGIVING "I think it's important that we recognize that these are not simply injustices of the past," Mejia continued. "And as a city, we have a responsibility to ensure that our commitment to equity and justice includes the Indigenous peoples whose lands we live on." Meanwhile, in nearby Plymouth — the famed site of the 1621 "first Thanksgiving" feast between the Pilgrims and the Wampanoag people, where the United American Indians of New England (UAINE) has held the annual National Day of Mourning every year since 1970 — town officials and organizers appeared in court Monday over a dispute about this year's event logistics. ARIZONA MAN THREATENED WITH ARREST FOR PREACHING AT HOLIDAY FESTIVAL FILES LAWSUIT The legal battle centers on a 1998 settlement, signed after a clash between police and demonstrators the year prior, that requires Plymouth to make a mobile stage available for the event. According to CBS Boston, town officials now say they will not set up a stage on state property without proof of insurance or an outside vendor, citing liability concerns, while UAINE argues the demand violates the decades-old agreement. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The Plymouth Independent reported that Plymouth Superior Court Judge Brian Glenny took the arguments under advisement Monday, leaving a ruling pending just days before Thursday's 57th annual gathering on Cole's Hill. According to the outlet, Glenny did not express when a ruling might come, though lawyers involved indicated he understands "time is of the essence." However, regardless, a UAINE leader told the Plymouth Independent that the event would continue as planned. "I can assure you we will be there Thursday," Mahtowin Munro told the local outlet.

articles.title: Todd Blanche calls Nvidia a ‘good corporate citizen’ while dodging questions on investigation
articles.summary: Attorney General Todd Blanche praised Nvidia as a “good corporate citizen” while sidestepping questions about the Justice Department’s role in the president’s controversial decision to push for the reinstatement of CEO Jensen Huang.
articles.body: Attorney General Todd Blanche on Tuesday praised Nvidia as a “good corporate citizen” while sidestepping questions about the Justice Department’s role in the president’s controversial decision to push for the reinstatement of CEO Jensen Huang. President Donald Trump told CNBC on Monday that he’d spoken to Blanche and “they did a pretty good investigation, and they felt that he himself was exonerated,” referring to Huang. Asked at an unrelated press conference about Trump’s remarks, Blanche said, “What the president said is that he talked to a lot of people going into the decision that he made to encourage the board to reinstate him,” before adding, “I’m not going to get into communications I have with the president about it.” He then said that what Trump was saying “is exactly right.” “To the extent that, that the department, that the Department of Justice had information that he was committing crimes or something like this, that is, that is, that’s just not, that’s something that I would have certainly told the president had it been true,” Blanche said. NBC News previously reported that Trump sought Blanche and Vice President JD Vance’s help in convincing Nvidia’s board to bring Huang back. An administration official said the attorney general told the president that the DOJ had no evidence of wrongdoing by Huang or the company. Trump and Vance gave Nvidia’s board information that informed its decision to reinstate Huang, a person familiar with the conversations said. The company’s announcement of the move cited input from “senior levels” of government that convinced the board members that Huang posted “no national security risk.” When asked if Huang — who’d resigned as CEO earlier this month after reports of extramarital affairs, including a relationship with an alleged Chinese spy — had been investigated, Blanche told reporters, “What does that mean?” “Had Huang been investigated for what?” he continued. “I don’t understand the question,” he said, adding, “It’s certainly not fair to him to just speculate about, about things or answer hypothetical questions. And so, so no.” Asked about whether an investigation into the the chip exporter, Singapore-based Megaspeed, that the alleged spy worked for was ongoing, Blanche continued in a similar vein. “I don’t know what you’re talking about,” he said. “So, we have hundreds, if not more, export investigations going at any time at the Department of Justice.” When a reporter pointed out that Blanche had said last week that he was looking into the Nvidia situation, he then said, “We look into things all the time.” “How do you look at things? You look at things by subpoenaing. You look at talking to witnesses, examining public information, and that’s the way you run investigations, and that’s the way this investigation was run,” Blanche said. Pressed on whether Nvidia or Jensen were aware of efforts to send high-tech chips to China, Blanche said, “Nvidia is a good corporate citizen.” “Obviously if Nvidia was, was the target or was subject to some criminal investigation, or they were obstructing or thwarting our investigation, then that wouldn’t be the message that, that the president is saying to the American people,” the attorney general said. FBI Director Kash Patel, who also attended the press conference on cyber scams, was asked what the agency had spoken to Huang about or whether it had information about the alleged spy. “I don’t have anything to add,” Patel said, without stepping up to the microphone.

articles.title: US House counsel denies backing controversial raid on Ilhan Omar’s home
articles.summary: Legal counsel challenges DOJ’s assertion of House’s involvement in controversial raid on Ilhan Omar’s home.
articles.body:
Washington, DC, United States – The US House’s general counsel has accused federal prosecutors of wrongly claiming in court that the chamber’s legal office backed a raid on the home of Representative Ilhan Omar.

Court documents unsealed on Monday evening show that in the lead-up to the early morning October 12 raid on Omar’s home in Washington, DC, US Magistrate Judge Matthew Sharbaugh ordered the Department of Justice to give the lawmaker an opportunity to assert that some materials taken by them are constitutionally protected because she is a sitting member of Congress.

Matthew Berry, the House’s top lawyer, was tasked with helping protect that constitutional separation of powers for lawmakers, under a provision of the Constitution referred to as the Speech or Debate clause.

At court before the raid on Omar’s house, the Justice Department alleged it had consulted Berry and received his backing. Federal prosecutors told the court that Berry’s office “refused to be involved in the search” and that, “echoing the United States’ position, explained that, in his view, Speech or Debate clause protections do not extend to a member’s private residence”.

Berry told Al Jazeera that the Justice Department’s claim that his refusal to be involved in the search meant he agreed with the department was “categorically false”.

Berry acknowledged that his office had responded to a Justice Department email on the eve of the raid, saying that his office would not be present during the operation itself, but pointed out that a court had ruled Omar’s representatives must be given the chance to assert the constitutional privilege over which items were taken from her home.

“The Department of Justice’s assertion that I refused to be involved in the search of Representative Ilhan Omar’s residence because I agreed with the Department that Speech or Debate Clause protections do not extend to a Member’s private residence is categorically false,” Berry said in a statement.

According to court documents, Judge Sharbaugh rejected federal prosecutors’ assertions that the key constitutional provision shielding lawmakers from turning over work-related materials did not apply to Omar’s home, saying “this court sees differently.”

The raid on Omar’s home was widely condemned by Democratic lawmakers, who said it was a dangerous intrusion by President Donald Trump that violated constitutional separation of powers.

Omar’s lawyers, in a letter to the Justice Department after the raid in October , had said, “This search was neither justified nor lawful.” They said investigators did not provide them with a copy of the warrant in advance, and seized her phone and passport, along with other materials from her home.

Omar’s office did not respond to a request for comment from Al Jazeera.

A federal raid on a sitting member of Congress’ home was “extremely unusual”, and it would be highly doubtful the House Office of General Counsel would not want to be involved, said Timothy Heaphy, a former federal prosecutor who served as lead counsel for the House committee that investigated the January 6, 2021 attacks on the US Capitol.

The House general counsel’s office “represents the institutional prerogatives of the House. If a committee subpoenas something and there is an objection, the House’s General Counsel litigates that … if there is a Speech and Debate issue, they generally are involved,” Heaphy said.

“They would certainly want a voice in protecting the Speech and Debate privilege for members, regardless of politics. They are supposed to be bipartisan.”

The administration of US President Donald Trump is investigating Omar over alleged immigration fraud, with the president and top officials calling for her to lose her US citizenship and be deported.

Omar became a naturalised US citizen in 2000 after fleeing Somalia with her family as a child, according to her House biography. She has repeatedly rejected allegations by conservative critics about her immigration status, which was also probed in 2019 during Trump’s first administration.

Above all, Bruce was a loving husband, a devoted father and grandfather, a man of faith and a rancher." articles.title: Biden admin weighed quitting Twitter after Elon Musk purchase, new HHS doc drop reveals
articles.summary: HHS launched a searchable public records trove with Robert F. Kennedy Jr.'s calendars and Biden-era memos, promising transparency for health agencies.
articles.body: Amid a push to bolster transparency, the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) launched a searchable trove of public records, including previously unreleased memos from the Biden administration and Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s calendars. While the website will be updated over time, the initial drop includes a Biden-era memo detailing how the National Institutes of Health (NIH) considered no longer having a presence on Twitter after billionaire Elon Musk acquired the platform in October 2022, renamed it X and promised to scale back moderation amid free expression concerns. Also included within the department's so-called Radical Transparency dashboard are Kennedy’s calendars, which reporters have previously requested and have not been publicly disclosed before now. HHS BUREAUCRATS ACCUSED OF 'SABOTAGING' RFK JR'S EFFORTS TO EXPOSE FAUCI RECORDS "When President Trump asked me to lead HHS, I promised to bring transparency back to the American health agencies," Kennedy said in a video announcing the launch of the website. "If the government makes decisions that affect your health, you deserve to see the evidence behind them. Not simply to be told, ‘trust the science.’" Kennedy claims that HHS’ previous method of presenting public records was disorganized and confusing to use. He said public accountability would be aided by consolidating the documents in one simplified dashboard. The Cabinet secretary noted that his department plans to upload more documents to the website during his tenure and the first drop includes previously available documents that are now easier to search and locate. TRUMP ORDERS FEDERAL CONTRACTORS TO ALERT WHITE HOUSE ON CONGRESSIONAL RECORD REQUESTS Though many on the political right are likely to hail the move as HHS’ increasing transparency efforts, Democrats have criticized the agency for lacking transparency under Kennedy's leadership. Congressional Democrats, for instance, have repeatedly said Kennedy stonewalls their oversight inquiries and claim that HHS, under his leadership, has provided incomplete responses to their questions. A letter sent by 18 Democratic lawmakers on Nov. 19, 2026, called out "an alarming lack of public transparency" following a delay to the disbursement of rural healthcare grants. In early 2025, HHS reduced staff working on Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) requests and public records at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and Food and Drug Administration (FDA) — another move Democrats claim stifles or at least slows transparency. Previous releases of public records by the Trump administration have enabled journalists to uncover millions of dollars in welfare fraud. President Donald Trump has charged Vice President JD Vance, seen by some as his heir apparent, with leading the White House charge against fraud, signaling the high importance of the issue to the administration. WHITE HOUSE LAUNCHES INTERACTIVE MAP TRACKING BILLIONS IN SUSPECTED FRAUD In addition to public records releases, HHS has also pushed regulations requiring that healthcare companies make more information public about their pricing practices. While the administration focuses on fraud, concerns about corruption within its ranks have taken root with voters amid press reports regarding conflicts of interest and alleged self-dealing. A Fox News survey found that 60% of Americans were concerned about government corruption ahead of the recent midterm elections.
