articles.title: CDC director draws doubts from employees and ire from legislators
articles.summary: NEW YORK (AP) — Three months into her tenure as head of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Dr. Erica Schwartz is being investigated by House Dem...
articles.body:
NEW YORK (AP) — Three months into her tenure as head of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Dr. Erica Schwartz is being investigated by House Democrats, facing a call to resign, and drawing ire from both within and outside the agency.

What's been happening at the nation's top public health agency has alarmed outside health professionals. It also has alienated staff, leaving morale as bad as ever, employees say.

Schwartz, 54, took the helm of the CDC at a very challenging time: the worst U.S. measles epidemic in more than three decades, a large dengue fever outbreak in Florida and the fastest-growing overseas Ebola outbreak in history.

She reports to U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who is a longtime critic of vaccines and federal public health policy and who played a role in decimating CDC staffing last year.

"She has a tough job, at a tough time, and a tough boss," said Noel Brewer, a University of North Carolina public health professor.

In an interview with The Associated Press on Tuesday, Schwartz defended her work, saying she's trying to restore trust in the CDC — including by changing how measles-associated deaths are being reported. She said some of the criticisms are based on misperceptions and argued she is making progress on her goals.

"I do understand why people have concerns," Schwartz told the AP from her home in Naples, Florida. "Have I made mistakes? Certainly. But I'm here to work on the behalf of the American people."

Some experts say she has made the situation worse. And critics are seizing on the Pan American Health Organization's declaration last week that measles is continuously spreading here, marking the re-establishment of a public health threat that was eliminated in the last century.

"I have no confidence that she will do what it takes to course-correct at the CDC, and she should resign immediately," said U.S. Sen. Michael Bennet, a Colorado Democrat.

When President Donald Trump nominated Schwartz to be the next CDC director in April, he called her "a STAR!" on social media.

She holds both medical and law degrees. She was chief medical officer for the U.S. Coast Guard, where she oversaw 41 clinics and 150 sick bays. She served as deputy surgeon general in the U.S. Public Health Service, helping to lead uniformed medical and health professionals posted at the CDC and government health agencies.

Many public health leaders were cautiously optimistic, noting the CDC badly needed steady leadership after enduring more than a year of turmoil and months of being led by interim directors.

Schwartz was the third Trump nominee for CDC director in less than 18 months. The first was a former Florida congressman whose nomination was pulled an hour before a Senate confirmation hearing. The second was Susan Monarez, who won Senate approval but then was ousted less than a month into the job when Trump administration officials said she was not aligned with the president's agenda.

Under Kennedy, the agency has seen around 30% of its staff leave, mostly through layoffs, resignations and retirements.

At her nomination hearing , Schwartz pledged "radical transparency" to rebuild public trust in the agency, which she noted declined during the COVID-19 pandemic and which has eroded further under Kennedy.

"I will always stand on science and speak the truth, even in difficult moments," she testified.

Meanwhile, public misperceptions about vaccines have persisted. A recent Annenberg Public Policy Center survey found that about 1 in 6 Americans said they believed that "vaccines given to children for diseases like measles, mumps and rubella cause autism" — even though dozens of studies have determined there's no causal link. Roughly another 1 in 5 said they didn't know whether it was true.

Schwartz started at the Atlanta-based agency in mid-August. A week later, she held her first "all hands" staff meeting , during which she promised to advocate for the agency and said she wouldn't hesitate to disagree with Kennedy — but only privately.

Some say that's when their optimism for Schwartz began to fade.

"I don't have a clear sense of what is important to her, what are her red lines," one CDC health scientist told the AP. "If we're talking about radical transparency," it is appropriate to know on what issues and what messaging she will not compromise, the scientist added. The employee spoke on condition of anonymity for fear of retribution.

Asked about that assessment, Schwartz said: "I would never do anything unethical or illegal. ... That is a red line."

Despite that transparency pledge, CDC and HHS officials for months would not release Schwartz's salary — even though it is public information. Schwartz is paid about $375,000 a year, CDC officials finally told the AP this week, above the typical range for previous CDC directors.

So far she also has been less visible than some predecessors. She has not held any news conferences, and has not used her bully pulpit to try to persuade more Americans to get vaccinations — including for measles, the flu and COVID-19.

Schwartz told the AP that, concerning measles, she doesn't believe a federal health official on TV will sway most of the unvaccinated.

But with the nation experiencing its worst measles epidemic in decades, many public health and medical leaders say Schwartz should be strongly urging Americans to get vaccinated.

"I hope to see her display independence from the vaccine rhetoric and challenges that have been part of this administration," said Dr. Wendy Armstrong, president of the Infectious Diseases Society of America. "I don't think we have seen that yet."

Kennedy continues to back Schwartz. The Health and Human Services Department issued a statement in response to Associated Press queries, quoting Kennedy as saying she had his full support.

"Dr. Schwartz brings the judgment to make hard decisions and the courage to see them through. She is reforming CDC and sharpening its focus on its core mission: protecting Americans from disease," the statement said.

Congressional Democrats are launching investigations

Some Democratic legislators accuse Schwartz and Kennedy of downplaying measles.

Kennedy has challenged health officials' accounts of measles deaths. And the CDC has stopped quickly relaying state reports of measles deaths. It adopted a new policy requiring the review of death certificates, which has resulted in CDC counting only about half the measles-associated deaths that states are reporting.

Schwartz said that was her decision, and stemmed from her desire to have a uniform definition of what counts as a measles death.

Democrats on the House Energy & Commerce Committee have questioned why CDC changed the policy.

"As the crisis worsens, we are concerned that you continue to direct an effort at CDC to downplay the outbreak and artificially reduce the number of deaths that CDC reports," according to a statement from Reps. Frank Pallone Jr. of New Jersey, Diana DeGette of Colorado and Yvette Clarke of New York.

"We are expanding our investigation to examine the threats your actions pose to Americans' health and whether changes to your statutory authority are required," they added.

The statement followed a briefing at which Schwartz was supposed to answer congressional staffers' questions about the measles data. The committee leaders described Schwartz as unresponsive and, at times, misleading.

Schwartz argued that she was "fully transparent. And I am really concerned that they think there is more to the story. There isn't."

CDC employees see little sign of progress

The AP interviewed eight current CDC workers about Schwartz's tenure. They all spoke on condition of anonymity, saying they feared retribution for speaking frankly about what's going on within the agency.

Some said they never had high expectations. Others said they initially were hopeful but lost confidence, some of them blaming her handling of the measles death count. One said it's still too early to judge her.

Several said they had hoped for more improvements and stability. Announcements about leadership appointees coming, going and changing titles have continued in a blur, the employees told the AP.

Some mentioned Caroline DeBerry, a former vice president at a conservative think tank and author of independently published novels including one titled "Esther: The Woman Who Didn't Know Her Place."

DeBerry got a job as acting director of communications, starting in August. Employees said she gained notoriety within the agency when all CDC website updates ground to a halt while awaiting her approval.

Asked about it, Schwartz said: "There was a bit of clunkiness that happened one day." She also said DeBerry is on "terminal leave" and her last day will be in December, but did not immediately offer additional detail.

None of the agency veterans interviewed by the AP said they have spoken with Schwartz. But some said they had seen her around the CDC campus accompanied by a group of security guards.

Security has been a sensitive topic at CDC, especially since an August 2025 shooting outside the entrance of CDC's main campus. A Georgia man who had blamed the COVID-19 vaccine for making him depressed and suicidal opened fire, killing a police officer and spraying bullets into 150 windows .

(The slain officer, David Rose, is widely held up as a hero by CDC employees, and some expressed irritation that Schwartz referred to him as "Officer Stone" during a recent health summit appearance.)

Dr. Tom Frieden, who served as CDC director in the Obama administration, said he occasionally had an escort outside the CDC campus after he received death threats. But Schwartz moves with a large security team inside CDC, and agency staffers said they don't recall seeing that before.

"It feels like they're afraid of us," one health scientist said.

Schwartz acknowledged that early in her time at CDC, she walked the halls accompanied by about a half dozen guards at the recommendation of security leadership. The security details have been reduced to one plainclothes guard, she said.

Confusion over the publication of scientific reports

A directive about research publications shows just how far apart CDC staff feel from the political leadership.

Two CDC scientists told the AP that they were directed in a recent meeting to stop submitting their research to journals run by organizations that have sued Kennedy. The prohibition would cover Pediatrics, one of the most-cited journals for doctors who specialize in children's medical care, and Clinical Infectious Diseases, a highly regarded publication for doctors focused on germs.

The scientists said the directive was clearly stated but not written down in a memo or email.

HHS and CDC officials are adamant that neither Kennedy nor any other HHS or CDC official ever issued such a directive.

At the health summit, Schwartz acknowledged that CDC employees have lost trust in the political appointees who have been put in charge of the agency, "and I'm trying to earn that trust every day."

She talked about work going on to stabilize the agency's leadership and develop a "strategic hiring plan" for 2027.

CDC employees look around and see burned-out colleagues.

"I think everyone is just exhausted," one health scientist said. "There's just a sense that we can't go on like this anymore."

articles.title: Kamala Harris' former political mentor and boyfriend delivers stinging warning about 2028 comeback
articles.summary: Willie Brown says Kamala Harris is "not a communicator" and doesn't want her to run in 2028, as Pete Buttigieg and Gavin Newsom eye the Democratic primary.
articles.body: Willie Brown, a longtime California Democrat and a power broker in the state party, said former Vice President Kamala Harris lacks the communication skills needed to run for president again in 2028. "She’s not a communicator," Brown said in an interview with Tara Palmeri, an independent journalist. "No Baptist preacher flavor in her soul," he added. Although Harris remains one of the country’s most recognizable Democratic figures, Brown’s skepticism comes from a longtime political ally and casts doubt on her potential candidacy. DEMOCRATS SHY AWAY FROM QUESTIONS ON WHETHER HARRIS SHOULD RUN FOR PRESIDENT IN 2028 "I’m sorry that she even thinks about running for president. I don’t want her to run," Brown said. "She’s reached the highest electoral level for any woman in America," he added, referring to her post as President Joe Biden’s vice president. Brown, who once served as San Francisco mayor and California state Assembly speaker, has a long history with Harris. Early in her career, he appointed her to the California Unemployment Insurance Appeals Board and then the Medical Assistance Commission. The two were also romantically involved between 1994 and 1995. Brown, in a San Francisco Chronicle op-ed, openly discussed their relationship and his role in her political career in an article titled, "Sure, I dated Kamala Harris. So what? " GAVIN NEWSOM SAYS HE WON'T RUN FOR PRESIDENT IN 2028 IF KAMALA HARRIS RUNS "Yes, we dated. It was more than 20 years ago. Yes, I may have influenced her career by appointing her to two state commissions when I was Assembly speaker," Brown wrote. "And I certainly helped with her first race for district attorney in San Francisco. I have also helped the careers of House Speaker Nancy Pelosi, Gov. Gavin Newsom, Sen. Dianne Feinstein and a host of other politicians," he added. Representatives for Harris did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Fox News Digital about Brown’s comments about her prospects for 2028. Several other Democrats have already hinted at their own interest in a 2028 bid, crowding the potential field. Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., a top progressive in the House of Representatives, has hinted at a run. Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg has said he is "inclined" to run, and California Gov. Gavin Newsom announced plans to decide on a presidential bid at the beginning of the new year. articles.title: Trump pauses turkey pardon to salute US troops guarding Strait of Hormuz: 'Watch over and protect'
articles.summary: President Donald Trump paused the White House turkey pardon to thank U.S. troops enforcing what he called the greatest naval blockade against Iran.
articles.body: President Donald Trump paused Tuesday's annual White House Thanksgiving turkey pardoning ceremony to offer a special tribute and thanks to U.S. service members defending the Strait of Hormuz and enforcing a naval blockade against Iran. Speaking from the White House South Lawn during the 79th National Thanksgiving Turkey presentation, Trump thanked American troops deployed overseas and praised those working to prevent Tehran from acquiring a nuclear weapon. "We want to say a special thank you to them, the people that are guarding the strait know or the blockade we call it," Trump said. "It’s a blockade, the greatest naval blockade in history." TRUMP DARES IRAN TO BREACH US PORT BLOCKADE AS TEHRAN REPORTEDLY READIES 14 OIL TANKERS Trump asserted that the U.S. maritime cordon has stopped every Iranian vessel from passing through since its establishment, save for a brief pause earlier in the standoff. "Not one Iranian ship has gotten through to the blockade since we established it, other than we had a little moratorium. And we learned that you can’t trust them," Trump said. "But not one ship from Iran has gotten through. Our naval blockade is the most incredible naval blockade, probably in the history of the world. It’s amazing." IRANIAN ‘GHOST FLEET’ FILMED EVADING US BLOCKADE EN ROUTE TO CHINA, UANI SAYS Trump also contended that U.S. forces have severely degraded Iran's conventional military capabilities and restored oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz to levels higher than before the conflict began. The U.S. naval blockade targeting vessels entering and leaving Iranian ports began in April amid the Strait of Hormuz crisis and resumed in July following a temporary pause. Before returning to the holiday ceremony, Trump offered a Thanksgiving prayer for deployed U.S. troops and expressed pride in the country. "And we send them all our best wishes, Thanksgiving, and is very special. It’s a very special time for me for a lot of reasons," Trump said. "And I ask God to watch over and protect all of our military and all of our people. I’m so proud of our people, and I’m so proud to be your president because we’ve never had a time like this." articles.title: Obama judge's Omar warrant unsealing directly contradicts his own decision in Trump case, DOJ says
articles.summary: Justice Department lawyers say Judge James Boasberg contradicted his ruling by unsealing search warrant records in Rep. Ilhan Omar's Washington, D.C. case.
articles.body: Government lawyers argue unsealing documents related to the warrant used to search the Washington, D.C., home of Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., is at odds with a ruling made by the same Obama-appointed federal judge in a high-profile case against President Donald Trump. Lawyers for the Justice Department pleaded in the filings with Judge James Boasberg, who has frequently found himself at odds with the Trump administration, not to unseal search warrant materials in the Omar case due to the ongoing nature of the investigation,. The DOJ also argued it has not yet finished executing that search warrant. Still, Boasberg ordered last week the redacted documents to be released. The DOJ submitted their redacted and the materials were made public Monday night. The only document Boasberg ordered to remain sealed was the government's affidavit presented to a magistrate court judge in order to secure the search warrant. 'RADICAL LEFT LUNATIC' JUDGE TRUMP WANTED IMPEACHED TAKES UP ILHAN OMAR WARRANT FIGHT "Just a few years ago, Chief Judge Boasberg ruled that search warrant proceedings and related documents should not be made open to the public while an investigation is ongoing," the DOJ said in an emergency ex parte brief in opposition to the unsealing. "The Chief Judge was merely echoing many other courts—like the D.C. Circuit, the Ninth Circuit, the Fourth Circuit, and others when he said that," the brief continued. The case to which the DOJ referred — where Boasberg ruled that search warrant documents should remain under seal during active investigations — was none other than Special Counsel Jack Smith's probe into Trump for alleged election interference after his 2020 presidential loss, and for the alleged retention of classified documents. Trump was indicted in both of those investigations. All the charges were eventually dropped. ILHAN OMAR RECORDS SHOW JUDGE, DOJ OFFICIALS DEBATING BEFORE RAID OF HOME In that case, like the Omar case, media organizations sought to unseal a warrant related to the search. Specifically, the press wanted to view a warrant obtained by Smith related to Twitter's records associated with Trump's account, @realDonaldTrump. Boasberg's tune was much different in that case, when, like in the Omar case, the government asked him to keep the warrant under seal due to the ongoing nature of the case. Notably, Trump had already been indicted when Boasberg ruled that the records needed to remain sealed while Omar has not been indicted. "Ultimately, the undeniable need to protect an ongoing criminal investigation tips the balance toward the Government’s request to continue sealing," Boasberg wrote in his Nov. 29, 2023 ruling. The White House did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment on the apparent u-turn from the judge. In the Omar case, government lawyers said they weren't opposed to releasing the documents at an appropriate future date, but did not want them unsealed while the case is ongoing. Boasberg didn't find that argument compelling. But in the case against Trump, he did. "There may yet come a time when press access becomes appropriate, but at present the Application is a premature bid for sensitive information pertaining to an active investigation," he wrote in 2023. Throughout his 2023 ruling in favor of the government's bid to keep the warrant in the Trump case sealed, Boasberg continually noted the government's ability to keep warrants under seal. ILHAN OMAR HUDDLES WITH HER DC-BASED LAWYERS DURING HER FIRST DAY BACK ON CAPITOL HILL AMID FEDERAL PROBES He said in a second instance: "When it comes to an active investigation, the Government 'has always been able to restrict access to warrant materials by requesting a sealing order, which courts have granted freely upon a showing that a given criminal investigation requires secrecy,'" Boasberg's ruling said. In response to the media's claim that the First Amendment should be a deciding factor in unsealing the Trump warrant, Boasberg disagreed. "The historical practice is somewhat muddled, but it suggests that the First Amendment does not open search warrants and related documents to public examination when an investigation is ongoing. Search-warrant applications traditionally have been filed ex parte and thus out of the public’s view." The DOJ confirmed in a brief statement to Fox News Digital on Tuesday that the characterization that Boasberg contradicted himself in unsealing the Omar documents "is accurate and a point we have made in our court filings." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP One issue distinguishing Boasberg's ruling in the 2023 Trump case from the Omar case is the Constitution's Speech or Debate Clause, which shields lawmakers from certain government intrusions into their legislative work. In the Omar case, the Justice Department argued that searching her home did not involve those protections. Magistrate Judge Matthew Sharbaugh disagreed and required safeguards for potentially privileged materials. Boasberg later questioned why the legal arguments over those constitutional protections should remain sealed when sensitive investigative details could be redacted. He nevertheless agreed to keep the government's warrant affidavit sealed to protect the ongoing investigation. Boasberg has also faced scrutiny over investigative secrecy during the Biden-era Arctic Frost probe, when he signed nondisclosure orders tied to subpoenas for Republican lawmakers' phone records. Unlike the Omar and Trump rulings, those orders restricted telecommunications companies from revealing the subpoenas rather than deciding whether court documents should be made public. Court officials have said Boasberg may not have known lawmakers' records were involved. The District Court for the District of Columbia declined to comment. The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Columbia did not return a request for comment. Omar's home was raided in the early morning hours of Oct. 12, 2026. Fox News Digital confirmed that the investigators are probing whether Omar or her father fraudulently filled out her citizenship paperwork, though the full scope of the investigation remains under wraps. The unsealing of last night's documents revealed that investigators are seeking evidence dating back as far as 1980, and that investigators believe Omar committed "crimes over decades— beginning long before she was ever in Congress."

articles.title: Florida official addresses 'misimpression' about teen son's fatal campsite shooting
articles.summary: Florida official Joe Vinson says whoever fatally shot his 19-year-old son inside a tent near Blackwater River aimed deliberately and "laughed" while fleeing.
articles.body: A newly elected Florida official is speaking out to correct what he called a "misimpression" about the fatal shooting of his 19-year-old son during a weekend camping trip, alleging whoever fired the shots aimed deliberately at an occupied sandbar and "laughed as they drove away." In an Instagram post Tuesday, Escambia County Commissioner Joe Vinson mourned his son, Carey Washington Vinson, who was known as "Wash," while sharing new details about the Sunday night shooting along the Blackwater River in the Florida Panhandle. "I need to correct a misimpression you might have gotten about the shooting," Joe Vinson said. "This was not a freak hunting accident — not someone firing carelessly in the dark. It was not a ‘stray bullet’ that killed our Wash." According to Joe Vinson, the shooter or shooters stood on the opposite riverbank, close enough to see the group's campfire and hear them talking, and aimed at the occupied campsite. NEWLY ELECTED FLORIDA COMMISSIONER'S SON SHOT DEAD INSIDE TENT DURING CAMPING TRIP "As we understand it, some person(s) stood on the opposite bank of the river and pointed a gun at the sandbar campground, knowing it was occupied," Joe Vinson said. "They were close enough to see the campfire and hear people talking. They fired shot after shot with malicious intent, and after a pause when the panicked campers screamed ‘stop,’ they fired another volley, then laughed as they drove away." Law enforcement officials have provided few details about the shooting. First responders were dispatched to the Blackwater River area Sunday after a 911 call. Deputies found the 19-year-old inside his tent with a gunshot wound to the head and pronounced him dead, according to the Santa Rosa County Sheriff's Office. Wash Vinson and his friends had been camping on sandbars along the river since Friday, Santa Rosa County Sheriff's Office Chief Deputy Randy Tifft previously told People magazine. MARATHONER ASKED HUSBAND ABOUT ‘POWDERY’ WATER BEFORE FATAL FALL – THEN POLICE FOUND HIS GOOGLE SEARCHES In a Facebook update Tuesday, the Sheriff's Office issued an urgent plea for witnesses, asking anyone who saw suspicious activity near Deaton Bridge Road and Boat Ramp Road on Sunday to come forward. "Santa Rosa County, we need your assistance," the Sheriff's Office wrote. "Investigators continue to work diligently to identify those involved in the fatal shooting of Carey Vinson on November 22, 2026, and determine the circumstances that led to this tragic loss of life. "Our thoughts and prayers remain with the Vinson family during this incredibly difficult time. The Santa Rosa County Sheriff's Office remains committed to conducting a thorough investigation and bringing those responsible to justice." Joe Vinson, who made history earlier this year as the first non-party-affiliated county commissioner elected in Escambia County, first announced the tragedy on Monday, writing that his family was "shocked and heartbroken about our sweet boy." In his follow-up tribute, Joe Vinson remembered his son as a "sweet, thoughtful young man" and a history major at Florida State University who loved tabletop games, played Beethoven on the piano and Jeff Buckley on guitar and had just been accepted to a summer study-abroad program in Valencia, Spain. ALLEGED DRUNKEN DRIVER WAS OVER 3 TIMES THE LIMIT WHEN HE KILLED NEWLY ENGAGED WOMAN DAYS AFTER JAIL RELEASE "Most of all, he had a tender and loving heart — for his friends and family, for his girlfriend, for animals, for the marginalized. He was quick to laugh and easy to love. I can’t believe I’ll never feel his hugs again, or hear him bickering with his siblings. I can’t believe any of this. Every impatient moment, every unkind word, I will gladly take them back if you would just come back to us," Joe Vinson wrote. Joe Vinson urged anyone with information to contact the Santa Rosa County Sheriff's Office at 850-983-1190 or Crime Stoppers at 850-437-STOP. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "I know it won’t bring back Wash, but I would sleep better knowing they can’t hurt anyone else," he wrote. A spokesperson for the Santa Rosa County Sheriff's Office told Fox News Digital Tuesday that "any information, no matter how small it may seem, could be valuable to this investigation." Fox News Digital attempted to reach Joe Vinson for further comment.

articles.title: Ilhan Omar’s legal reckoning is looming, and redactions can't hide it
articles.summary: The DOJ says Rep. Ilhan Omar committed crimes over decades, and newly released search warrant documents hint at fraud charges or denaturalization ahead.
articles.body: Some things are not a matter of if, but when. The potential for fraud charges against Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn. was made plain Monday night when a federal judge released to the public roughly 170 pages of legal documents in support of the judicially ordered search of her Washington, D.C., residence last month. The vast majority of the information contained therein was heavily redacted in a blizzard of blackness. It resembled an ink spill masquerading as a public record. But the dark chessboard still revealed spaces of valuable information that suggest an indictment of the Minnesota congresswoman may be forthcoming. GREGG JARRETT: ILHAN OMAR COULD FACE INDICTMENT, DENATURALIZATION AND DEPORTATION An alternative to criminal charges might be a lesser set of civil proceedings that could result in Omar’s denaturalization and deportation. Either way, a legal reckoning is looming. In one striking passage, the Department of Justice states, "The United States believes that Ilhan has committed (redacted) crimes over decades — beginning long before she was ever in Congress." WHAT'S NEXT FOR ILHAN OMAR? FORMER IMMIGRATION JUDGE BREAKS DOWN LEGAL RISKS AMID FEDERAL PROBES In another excerpt, the investigators referred to "evidence of violations occurring between 1980 and the present." In other words, there are purported deceptions that span decades. The suspected crimes identified in the filing have been blacked out. But we can reasonably fill in the blanks. — Immigration fraud: That Omar knowingly provided materially false information on immigration applications. — Citizenship fraud: That she made intentionally false representations to secure citizenship. — False statements: That she deliberately made materially false statements to federal officials on government documents. — Conspiracy: That she knowingly agreed with another person to commit a federal offense. — Conspiracy to obstruct justice: That she schemed with two or more people to conceal crimes. Omar has not yet been charged and flatly denies any wrongdoing. But the search of her home and other locations underscores an aggressive criminal investigation. ILHAN OMAR APPEARS CLUELESS ON BASIS FOR FEDERAL PROBES: ‘YOU PROBABLY HAVE MORE DETAILS ON THAT’ The reference by the feds to the year 1980 is illuminating. It indicates that they possess compelling evidence that Omar lied about her age to gain U.S. citizenship. She originally claimed that she was born in 1981, but later changed it to 1982 to allegedly support her story that she was a minor and thereby eligible for citizenship through her father. If it can be proved that Omar was already an adult, then any misrepresentation by her in naturalization paperwork that she was under the age of 18 would nullify her citizenship. It would also constitute fraud. Moreover, if Omar’s father never obtained legitimate citizenship himself, that would invalidate her citizenship, too. ILHAN OMAR HUDDLES WITH HER DC-BASED LAWYERS DURING HER FIRST DAY BACK ON CAPITOL HILL AMID FEDERAL PROBES There is also the matter of whether Omar married her brother so that he could gain immigration benefits. Marriage fraud is a federal felony governed by a five-year statute of limitations. But the clock can be extended under a variety of circumstances, including any ongoing efforts to conceal it. Regardless, there is no statute of limitations for civil immigration fraud. Omar has not yet been charged and flatly denies any wrongdoing. But the search of her home and other locations underscores an aggressive criminal investigation. Fox News has reported that federal authorities have obtained a DNA sample from Omar. The results have not been publicly disclosed. At present, it is unknown publicly whether she and her former husband, Ahmed Nur Said Elmi, are siblings. ILHAN OMAR'S TURBULENT WEEK EXPLAINED: THE DUELING PROBES THAT THREW THE SOMALI-BORN PROGRESSIVE INTO CHAOS In a recent interview, Omar was asked whether she engaged in a sham marriage to her brother. Her response was, "Not to my knowledge." That cautious and qualified answer was so strange that it only compounded suspicion. All of this raises the question of whether Omar used a false identity in immigration and citizenship documents. In earlier court filings — and repeated in Monday’s document disclosure — she is identified by the government as "Ilhan Nur Said Elmi, a.k.a. Ilhan Abdullah Omar." This indicates that the feds believe that she has been living her life under an alias and that her real birth name is the same surname as her alleged brother-husband. Records reportedly show that Omar’s late father also went by the name Nur Said Elmi. DNA test results would answer this vexing question. If Omar concealed her true name or identity, that would constitute both false statements and fraud. Criminal prosecution could follow, along with revocation of naturalization and removal proceedings. Supporters of Omar continue to make dubious arguments on her behalf. They claim that these are ancient allegations unjustly resurrected and barred by the statute of limitations. Not true. Every time Omar used her U.S. passport or relied on original false statements in updating any official paperwork would constitute a renewed set of crimes, resetting the statute of limitations. FEDERAL AGENTS SEIZE PHONE OF REP ILHAN OMAR IN RAID TIED TO IMMIGRATION FRAUD PROBE Finally, the repeated assertion by Omar that the investigation of her is politically motivated defies its origin. The first probe of her questionable marriage began under President Barack Obama in the summer of 2016. According to reporting by The New York Times, the result "found some evidence that it was fraudulent." Yet no action was taken. The same is true of a Biden administration investigation of Omar examining her marriage history and citizenship records. Again, no civil or criminal charges were ever brought, and the probe was buried from public view. Preferential treatment? Perhaps. The cover-up seems more political than the investigation itself. REP ILHAN OMAR'S IMMIGRATION HISTORY FACES NEW SCRUTINY AS FEDERAL INVESTIGATORS SUBPOENA RELATIVES Monday’s disclosure of documents, as sparse as they were, confirms the breadth and seriousness of the federal investigation. Of course, it does not offer conclusive evidence of Omar’s guilt. However, the government’s statement that it believes Omar committed crimes over the course of decades is extraordinary. Whether the various searches netted incriminating evidence beyond what the feds already have is unknown. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION The 67-page affidavit in support of the search warrant is still under seal. It would provide a very detailed narrative of what convincing evidence the government has and what crimes Omar may have violated. This pivotal document will probably remain sealed unless or until charges are brought. Without it, we do not know whether investigators have decisive documentary proof, credible witness testimony, and irrefutable DNA evidence that implicates Omar in criminal or civil wrongdoing that will lead to charges. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP But given the serious efforts to unravel the puzzle of Ilhan Omar’s suspicious past, it seems inevitable that answers will be forthcoming, and charges may well be brought. articles.title: How Democrats are gaming out the timing of their 2028 bids: From the Politics Desk
articles.summary: In today’s edition, Natasha Korecki explores when we might see Democratic presidential contenders launch their campaigns.
articles.body: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail. In today’s edition, Natasha Korecki explores when we might see Democratic presidential contenders launch their campaigns. Plus, Sahil Kapur interviews DSCC Chair Kirsten Gillibrand about the 2028 Senate map. Programming note: We are taking a holiday break the rest of the week and will be back in your inbox on Monday. Have a happy Thanksgiving! — Adam Wollner How Democrats are gaming out the timing of their 2028 bids Analysis by Natasha Korecki Now that the midterm elections are all of three weeks behind us, Democratic White House hopefuls can get real about their 2028 campaigns. With that comes one of the first big decisions they’ll need to make: exactly when to enter the race. Jump in early and face the harsh national spotlight and a possibility of burning through cash too soon. Wait too long and risk getting left behind in what’s expected to be a crowded field. We talked to advisers to potential candidates, donors and outside strategists who laid out the major considerations that go into deciding the right moment to officially announce a campaign for president. Here are some of the key factors to keep an eye on. A mad rush in two phases: Several strategists said to expect to see two main phases of rollouts (with the potential of it starting even before the end of the year). The first is in January, after the new party superstars in Congress settle in. And the second is in February and March, with the bulk of the field likely to be in place by March 31, just as the first quarter of fundraising ends. “The minute you jump in, you need to start paying people, raising money, all of those things,” a senior Democratic strategist who worked on a presidential campaign in 2020 said. “But time is also your friend in a crowded field. … You need to distinguish yourself.” Governing: Voters just re-elected Govs. Josh Shapiro in Pennsylvania, JB Pritzker in Illinois and Gov. Wes Moore in Maryland to four-year-terms. It’s unlikely they’d announce before their own January swearing-in ceremonies. And they might even have to clear legislative sessions and state of the state addresses from their plates first. Money: Locking down donors is vital to demonstrate fundraising strength early. Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear is asking his donors to convene in December before any decision happens. Some potential contenders, like Arizona Sen. Mark Kelly, are already sitting on a pile of cash. And while Pritzker, a notorious self-financier, is expected to fundraise for the first time, the billionaire can reliably lean on personal wealth. Staffing up: Some nascent campaigns have already locked down their hired guns, but with so many Democrats competing for talent, there are some potential contenders still wrangling over some important hires. “There are a lot of factors,” said a person working with a potential 2028 candidate. “It’s a conversation I know everybody is having.” Book releases: Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg is due out with a book in January. Moore has a scheduled March release for his book. Conventional wisdom (though it isn’t always accurate) is that candidates will seek to tap into momentum from the publishing tours to then shift into campaign mode. The X factors: As we reported this week, what Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., and former Vice President Kamala Harris decide to do looms particularly large over the rest of the field. Someone like Rep. Ro Khanna may want to jump in sooner rather than later to get a leg up in the progressive lane over AOC. For his part, California Gov. Gavin Newsom has said he would not run for president if Harris does — though not everyone is buying that. “When he said it, it was total bull----,” said billionaire Democratic donor John Morgan. “Put this down for my prediction: Even if she runs, he’s running.” 🔵 Related: Democrats grumble about the DNC’s plan for the 2028 primary debates, by Jonathan Allen and Natasha Korecki DSCC chair says it’s ‘definitely possible’ for Democrats to win 60 Senate seats in 2028 By Sahil Kapur Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, D-N.Y. is seeking another two-year term as chair of the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee after her party flipped nine seats on its way to securing a 56-seat majority. In an interview with NBC News, Gillibrand said she’s bullish that Democrats can expand the map again in 2028, calling it “definitely possible” to capture 60 seats and win a very rare, filibuster-proof majority. “It’s on the table. There’s some easy targets that I’m very excited about — obviously, Wisconsin and North Carolina,” Gillibrand said. “But I would also suggest any state that was in play last cycle is in play this cycle. Waves tend to be two cycles long, and this is a very large blue tsunami.” If Democrats hold all their seats in 2028, their best pickup opportunities are seats in the highly competitive states of Wisconsin (held by Sen. Ron Johnson) and North Carolina (held by Sen. Ted Budd). From there the hill gets steeper, requiring victories in redder states. “I think we can put a lot of these states that we put in play last time that are exciting states like Kansas and South Carolina and Iowa,” all of which Democrats won in November, Gillibrand said. “There’s no reason why we can’t find extraordinary candidates, again, who have the right message to fight for their states to run in these very red and purple places.” Read more → That’s all From the Politics Desk for now. Today’s newsletter was compiled by Adam Wollner. If you have feedback — likes or dislikes — email us at politicsnewsletter@nbcuni.com And if you’re a fan, please share with everyone and anyone. They can sign up here.

articles.title: President of blue-collar coalition demanding higher pay, calls 'sub-minimum wage' a 'direct legacy of slavery'
articles.summary: One Fair Wage President Saru Jayaraman says the $2.13 tipped subminimum wage is a legacy of slavery as Democrats push a $25 living wage on Capitol Hill.
articles.body: One Fair Wage President Saru Jayaraman, who leads a coalition of lawmakers and blue-collar workers demanding a higher minimum wage, argued that paying a livable wage is an issue of racial and social justice. "The subminimum wage for tipped workers is a direct legacy of slavery. It was created after emancipation," Jayaraman told Fox News Digital on Monday, arguing that the policy was designed "to allow restaurants to hire newly freed Black people for free, not pay them, and make them live on tips." "Today, tipped workers are overwhelmingly women, single moms who work in restaurants like IHOP, Denny's and Chili's, struggle with three times the poverty rate, use food stamps at double the rate and suffer from the highest rates of sexual harassment because they have to put up with so much from customers to get tips. PROGRESSIVES UNVEIL $25 MINIMUM WAGE PUSH TO SOLVE AFFORDABILITY CRISIS DESPITE ECONOMIST INFLATION WARNING "So, what is social and racial justice?" she continued. "It is about allowing people to meet the cost of living. Everybody — White, Black, male, female — everybody deserves to earn enough to feed their families, and everybody deserves to earn that wage from their boss rather than having to put up with all kinds of crap from customers to get it from customers. Tips should be on top of a wage, as they are in several states, not instead of a wage." One Fair Wage joined House Democrats and restaurant workers on Capitol Hill Nov. 18 to urge the incoming 120th Congress "to answer the affordability election with a $25 living wage and to make the Living Wage for All Act a Day One priority." The current federal minimum wage has been set at $7.25 an hour since 2009, while the federal subminimum cash wage for tipped workers has remained frozen at $2.13 an hour since 1991. One Fair Wage is part of a national coalition of more than 100 organizations — including teachers' unions and progressive lawmakers — pushing for the $25 federal floor. DEMOCRATS SEIZE ON MIDTERM WINS TO PUSH MASSIVE MINIMUM WAGE HIKES, BUT ECONOMISTS SEE TROUBLE AHEAD 'CRAZY': MODERATES FEAR DEM LEADERSHIP PROMISED FAR-LEFT REPARATIONS AND ICE DEMANDS IN TURN OF VOTES The Living Wage for All Act (H.R. 8555), introduced in April by lead sponsor Rep. Delia Ramirez, D-Ill., alongside co-leads, including Rep. Analilia Mejia, D-N.J., would phase in a $25 minimum wage over several years — reaching $25 for large employers by 2031 and smaller businesses by 2038 — while eliminating subminimum wage carve outs for tipped workers. Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., introduced a companion bill in the Senate. Mejia, a progressive backed by Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., and Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., has championed far-left policies, including Medicare-for-all, a wealth tax and the abolition of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). The proposal, which would more than triple the current federal minimum wage, has raised concerns among critics and economists about potential job losses and the impact on small businesses in states with significantly lower living costs than major coastal cities. "We should be rallying around $25 at minimum, and it should be cost-adjusted for inflation so that people can have a job that enables them to survive and thrive," Rep. Everton Blair Jr., D-Ga., told Fox News Digital on the day of the news conference. FEDERAL $25 MINIMUM WAGE MANDATE WOULD DESTROY NEARLY 5M JOBS, HIT BOOMING SUN BELT HARDEST: STUDY Asked whether a nationwide $25 minimum wage could hurt workers and businesses in lower-cost states, Blair argued that the proposed rate should serve as a national baseline. He said $25 an hour should be "the floor" and "should be higher in places with a higher cost of living." Blair acknowledged concerns that raising the minimum wage could contribute to inflation but said lawmakers must find a way to increase workers' earnings while "keeping people afloat." Jayaraman described the Nov. 3 midterm elections — in which Democrats captured majorities in both the House and the Senate — as a "blue-collar wave mandate" demanding a $25 federal minimum wage. She argued the push transcends racial and partisan lines and urged both Republicans and Democrats to listen to their constituents. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP However, when the new Congress takes office in January, Democrats will remain well short of the two-thirds supermajority required in each chamber to override a presidential veto, setting the stage for messaging bills aimed at forcing President Donald Trump to reject progressive legislation.

articles.title: Authorities drop criminal charge against incoming House Democrat over unreturned rental car
articles.summary: The summons for Rep.-elect LaKesha Womack was issued in 2020, but law enforcement didn’t serve the warrant until last month, at a campaign event, court records show.
articles.body: Prosecutors in North Carolina announced Tuesday that they are dropping a 2020 felony charge against Democratic Rep.-elect LaKesha Womack, who flipped a House seat this month, over allegations that she failed to return a rental car. Womack was charged six years ago after a vehicle first rented by Womack in August 2019 was not returned to Budget Car Rental, according to Mecklenburg County District Attorney Spencer Merriweather. Merriweather said in a news release that Womack renewed the rental two more times over the next few months but never returned the car. Instead, it was returned in December 2019 after law enforcement agents recovered the vehicle, he said. Womack’s attorney, Harold Cogdell Jr., said in a statement Tuesday that his client had been “unaware a criminal summons had been issued” for “almost seven years.” “Upon learning of this unresolved matter, Ms. Womack promptly and fully resolved this matter with the rental car company,” Cogdell said. “The vehicle was returned to the owner, undamaged, forty-one days prior to the charge being issued on January 14, 2020.” According to the court documents, the summons was first issued in 2020, though it was not served until last month, when law enforcement officers provided Womack with the warrant at a campaign event on Oct. 11. It is not clear why it took years to deliver the summons. Merriweather said Tuesday that the state moved to voluntarily dismiss the charge against Womack after his office was informed on Nov. 16 that she had reached an agreement with Budget. Merriweather said his office confirmed that Budget had received “a sum of money” from Womack that was “equal to an assessed rental cost from the day the vehicle was deemed overdue until the day it came back into the possession of the victim corporation.” Representatives for Budget then “explicitly” said that they did not wish to continue with prosecution as it considered the matter resolved, Merriweather said. Budget did not immediately respond to a request for comment Tuesday. According to the court summons, the car was valued at $20,000. Womack has previously talked about experiencing housing insecurity after she moved back to Charlotte, North Carolina, in 2016, saying she lived in a hotel for a period of time and did not have a regular address for receiving mail. After receiving the summons during a campaign event last month, Womack criticized the timing of the move. “In the seven years that this has been kind of lingering, Mecklenburg County couldn’t find me or, you know, send me any paperwork?” Womack said in an Oct. 12 interview with the NAACP’s Gastonia branch. The felony charge was used in campaign ads that sought to boost GOP Rep. Tim Moore, who lost his re-election bid to Womack. “LaKesha Womack talks about integrity, but she’s charged with a felony,” one ad said. “Served a court summons at a campaign rally. Her court date: a week after the election.” “Don’t let Democrats hand this seat to a felony defendant,” the ad continued. Womack won North Carolina’s 14th Congressional District in the midterm elections by 2.2 percentage points, with the district swinging 17 points to the left compared with the 2024 election. She bested Moore, who was running for a second term, with a progressive campaign that emphasized affordability and healthcare. Her victory contributed to Democrats’ sweep in the midterm elections, where they won both the House and Senate. As of Tuesday, Democrats will hold 259 of the House’s 435 seats in January after flipping 47 seats, losing only three.

articles.title: US preparing to unveil new tariffs on global trading partners
articles.summary: The new levies would hit many of America's biggest trading partners, including China and the EU.
articles.body:
The US is preparing to announce new tariffs on several countries, the BBC understands.

The new import taxes would hit many of America's biggest trading partners, with China, the European Union, Mexico and Japan among the 16 jurisdictions affected.

The move comes after the White House's so-called "Section 301" investigation. It was launched in March after the US Supreme Court ruled that President Donald Trump's Liberation Day tariffs were illegal .

Trump has made tariffs a signature policy of his presidency, arguing that they will help boost American manufacturing and create jobs.

The president sent shockwaves around the world when he unveiled sweeping tariffs on global trading partners in April 2025 shortly after his return to the White House.

While the tariffs were later struck down, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer argued then that overproduction abroad was displacing American manufacturing and deterring investment.

Under the new tariffs, countries will face different import tax rates depending on the deals that they have previously struck with Trump.

The announcement is likely to increase tensions between the US and China, the world's two biggest economies, who remain locked in a trade dispute.

Despite last week's meeting between Trump and President Xi Jinping, the two sides have yet to fully resolve their difference with an interim agreement set to expire on 10 January.

In the run up to the Shenzhen summit the US accused China of not fully living up the terms of what it agreed in South Korea in October 2025.

Washington said Beijing was falling short on its commitments, "particularly as they relate to agricultural purchases, rare earths, and other critical minerals".

However earlier on Tuesday China extended the suspension of a ban on exports critical minerals including gallium, germanium, antimony until 27 January. The ban would otherwise have come into force on Friday.

The Trump administration's tariff policy has been criticised for putting up prices for American consumers and damaging the global economy.
